extracted.intended_audience: legal counsel, courts, and newswire/journalism professionals (news service operators, editors)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and operational conventions for wire-service news handling (labels, precedence, machine operation, office protocols) as shown in affidavit evidence from a 1916 Associated Press vs. International News Service dispute. Covers how bulletins/flashes are labeled, how updates are transmitted, and proper handling of received copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bulletin — designation of important/pressing news
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'Bulletin' preceding such despatch indicates in news service parlance that the news is of a particularly important and pressing character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to mark especially important items sent over the wire (examples in the text show many 'Bulletin' prefaced despatches). Editors and wire operators treat 'Bulletin' items as urgent; they are printed and delivered rapidly. Anti-pattern: failing to mark urgent items as 'Bulletin' risks under-prioritizing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flash — highest-importance telegram with absolute precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: A flash is one of the most important telegrams and indicates that the news is of the highest importance, and such a message has precedence over everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flashes (examples: in re Adamson law) preempt other traffic on the wire and must be given immediate attention and distribution. Operationally, flashes override normal scheduling and are handled first. Anti-pattern: delaying or not giving precedence to a 'Flash' message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of labels for updates: 'Follow', 'Add', 'Sub', 'Insert', 'Lead'
rubrics_metrics.description: Wire messages use labels such as 'Follow', 'Add', 'Sub', 'Bulletin lead', 'Bulletin insert', and 'Follow London' to indicate follow-ups, additions, substitutions, or rewritten leads to prior despatches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These markers tell receiving editors/operators how the new text relates to prior wire copy (e.g., 'Add' supplies extra material; 'Sub' supplies a substitute/updated bulletin; 'Follow' indicates continuation). Examples in the affidavits show many uses: 'Follow London', 'Add Chemung, N. Y.', 'Sub Toledo fire bulletin and add.' Proper handling requires recognizing and applying these labels rather than treating each as a stand‑alone story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rewrite or bypass central bureau for local rewrites
rubrics_metrics.description: Reprimand: 'Under no circumstances ever put out such bulletin again. We have bureau in Birmingham. Message us only. Do not rewrite anything.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local offices or managers should not re‑publish or rewrite bureau bulletins intended to be handled by the central bureau; instead they must message the central bureau and await instructions. Anti-pattern: sending rewritten bulletin directly out on the wire or to clients without coordinating with the bureau (as Ward was reprimanded for).

rubrics_metrics.name: Code words and ciphers to indicate competing services or sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of code words to indicate other services: e.g., 'Apathy' was the code word used to indicate The Associated Press; 'Ansonia' was another code word used by International News Service for The Associated Press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operators and editors use prearranged code words and office calls within internal messages to refer to competing services or bureaus discreetly. Examples in the transcript show messages like 'B F Apathy Kansas City flash says...' and 'B F Ansonia has: Bulletin.' Proper practice requires knowledge of the codebook and use of codes in internal coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office/office-call abbreviations and initials in internal wire messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal messages use initials and office calls (examples: 'B F' is Barry Faris, 'D R' indicates the Cleveland office, 'B X' is Detroit office, 'N. Y.' for New York) to identify senders/receivers and offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These shorthand identifiers are used in terse wire-to-wire messages to route and attribute information quickly. Operators must know the meaning of calls/initials to interpret messages correctly. Misreading these can cause routing or attribution errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive delivery and handling of Associated Press (AP) printed sheets
rubrics_metrics.description: The Morkrum apparatus prints news transmitted from the central office of The Associated Press into offices of member morning newspapers; 'an employee of The Associated Press is in constant attendance upon each of such receiving machines, and, as rapidly as the news is printed, delivers the sheet containing such news to the editor of the morning newspaper.' Sheets containing news furnished by The Associated Press are delivered for exclusive use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receiving-machine output (AP copy) is considered exclusive to member papers and should be attended and delivered by AP staff directly to editors. The affidavit describes employees of other services entering editorial rooms and taking notes/copies as improper behavior (seen as misappropriation). Best practice: prevent unauthorized access; AP attendant must control distribution. Anti-pattern: other-service editors copying bulletin sheets from machine or engaging editors to read copy aloud for note-taking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morkrum receiving machine operational practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The Morkrum receiving machine prints transmitted news on sheets; AP attendants 'inspect' and 'make repairs' as needed and 'deliver the sheet containing such news to the editor' immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machines must be kept in working order and attended by service staff; printed news is to be promptly handed to the appropriate editor. Technicians routinely inspect machines and may be in editorial rooms during evening/night hours; presence of technicians and attendants is normal. Operational detail: attendants relieve each other on schedules; machines produce copy for editors in near-real time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wire operating schedule / operator downtimes
rubrics_metrics.description: The wire of the International News Service is not operated between approximately 11.45 a.m. and 12.15 p.m. as the operators are at lunch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wire services may have predictable short downtimes (e.g., operator lunch breaks) that affect message timing. Editors and bureaus must account for these windows when expecting or sending time-sensitive copy. Anti-pattern: assuming continuous operation 24/7 without accounting for scheduled downtimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution and crediting of wire copy to the originating service
rubrics_metrics.description: The transcript documents instances where newspapers reproduced wire bulletins 'in precisely the same form' as the message 'sent out by the New York office of the International News Service, and was credited to the International News Service.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receiving newspapers should credit copy to the originating wire service as appropriate. Conversely, misuse or misattribution (reprinting another service's exclusive bulletins without permission) is treated as improper. The affidavit uses such examples to show distribution practices and alleged misappropriation.
